analysis.one_liner: Redirects antidumping tariff revenues to US companies that filed the trade complaints.
analysis.headline: 27 senators backed the bill, but after one committee hearing it died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change where antidumping and countervailing tariff money goes. Today those duties — paid by importers of goods found to be dumped or unfairly subsidized — flow into the Treasury. Under this bill they would be paid out every year to the American companies, farms, and ranches that filed the trade complaint, to cover things like equipment, research, health and pension benefits, and working capital. It would apply retroactively to duties assessed since October 1996.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic manufacturers, farmers, and ranchers that supported winning antidumping or countervailing duty petitions. Instead of the tariff money going to the Treasury, they would receive annual checks for qualifying business expenditures — plant, equipment, research and development, employer-paid health care and pensions, environmental equipment, raw materials, and borrowed working capital.

how_it_helps.text: Requires that duties collected under antidumping and countervailing duty orders be distributed annually to the affected domestic producers who brought the petition, for 'qualifying expenditures.'

Qualifying expenditures include plant, equipment, research and development, personnel training, technology acquisition, employer-paid health care and pension benefits, environmental equipment, raw materials and other inputs, and borrowed working capital needed to maintain production.
The payments would apply retroactively to antidumping and countervailing duty assessments made on or after October 1, 1996, so companies with existing orders could start collecting immediately.

The bill's stated rationale is that continued dumping keeps prices artificially low, leaving domestic producers reluctant to reinvest or rehire and unable to maintain employee pension and health benefits.

analysis.who_pays: The Treasury, and behind it general taxpayers, lose revenue that currently comes in from antidumping and countervailing duties. Consumers also bear indirect costs: the payments reward filing trade cases, which raises the volume of duties imposed on imported goods — costs that importers typically pass through in prices — and could invite retaliation from trading partners against US exports.

drawbacks.text: The bill converts government revenue into payments to private companies. Duties that currently go to the general Treasury would instead be routed to the petitioning firms, so taxpayers effectively fund a new subsidy to selected businesses.

Only the companies and worker representatives that supported the original petition are eligible — 'affected domestic producers' — so the money flows to the specific firms that brought each case, not to the industry broadly or to the workers as individuals (the qualifying expenditures are employer-paid categories like health and pension benefits).

By paying petitioners out of the duties their cases generate, the bill creates a standing financial incentive to file dumping and subsidy complaints, which would mean more tariffs on imported goods — costs that show up in consumer prices — and a likely flashpoint with US trading partners.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives a real benefit to a specific group — firms and farms that win trade cases — but the money comes from the public Treasury and the mechanism rewards filing trade complaints. The costs fall broadly on taxpayers and on buyers of imported goods, while the gains are concentrated on the petitioning companies. A well-designed version would have to answer why taxpayers, rather than the benefiting firms, should fund these payments.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, got one hearing in March 1999, and then sat with no further action until the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Mike DeWine introduced the bill on January 19, 1999, joined by seven original cosponsors, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance.
The Finance Committee held a hearing on the bill on March 23, 1999, printed as S.Hrg. 106-187.
After that hearing, no further action appears in the record — no markup, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never moved, the Treasury kept collecting antidumping and countervailing duties as general revenue, and consumers were spared a new incentive structure that would have generated more tariffs and more trade friction. The petitioning companies that would have received the payments are worse off than they would have been under the bill — though the idea resurfaced and passed in a later Congress by other means.

for.name: Mike DeWine
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled 26 cosponsors; original cosponsors included Hollings, Abraham, Santorum, Specter, Byrd, Hutchinson, and Voinovich.

for.name: 26 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan backing in the Senate.

for.name: Senate Finance Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on March 23, 1999 (S.Hrg. 106-187).

against.name: William V. Roth Jr.
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or reported the bill to the floor after the March 1999 hearing; no further action appears in the record for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 17 Republicans and 9 Democrats cosponsored — and the bill was stopped not by an opposing vote but by the Finance Committee simply never acting on it.

industries.industry: Domestic producers that file antidumping and countervailing petitions (manufacturers, farmers, ranchers)
industries.note: They would receive annual payouts of the tariff duties their petitions generate, covering plant, equipment, R&D, health and pension benefits, and working capital. Their gain comes directly out of Treasury revenue and out of a trade regime that keeps duties on imports — costs that land on taxpayers and consumers.

industries.industry: Importers and foreign exporters of goods subject to dumping or subsidy orders
industries.note: They would keep paying the same duties, but the bill would make the duty stream a payout to petitioners, strengthening the incentive to file more cases and raising the odds of foreign retaliation against US exports — pressure that ultimately falls on US businesses and consumers.
